source.title: Attributing and Exploiting Safety Vectors through Global Optimization in Large Language Models
source.authors: F. Chu; Jia-Hao Chen; Yuhong Wang; Jun Wang; Zhi-Hui Fu; Shou-Ling Ji; Songze Li

record.tranche_reason: The study’s interventions and overlap analyses argue for two spatially distinct attention-head safety pathways rather than a unified mechanism. This refines or challenges a monolithic account, but it does not test the original residual-stream direction method.
record.gate_note: The study intervenes on last-token attention-head activations selected by global optimization, not on a harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream difference-in-means direction. The overlap rates and the authors’ distinct-pathways conclusion bear on V4. The reported head-repatching behavior and perplexity results are recorded under fits_no_version because they do not test the residual-stream directions named by the versions. GOSV optimization losses and selection probabilities used to select heads are not outcome rows. The paper’s attack comparisons and alternative-patching comparison are not extracted as results for a claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper's own work is about attention-head repatching, which is not the residual-stream difference-in-means direction. Its only result on a claim version is the ORTHO baseline (Arditi et al. weight orthogonalization), run by the authors on four models. It is scored by HarmBench ASR on AdvBench and StrongREJECT (Table 2), with no-intervention ASR in Table 3. That is a new-setting result on V2 (weight-edit removal of refusal). The head-overlap results measure a different construct and do not bear on V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that the two strategies find spatially distinct head sets, meaning separate safety pathways rather than a unified mechanism. They report that safety is encoded in about 30% of heads and that their head-repatching attack beats white-box baselines, including ORTHO. They frame this as challenging a monolithic view of safety alignment.
record.recipe_differences: Uses global optimization to select attention heads, then repatches last-token head activations with harmful-example mean activations or zeros. It does not find a harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream direction or project that direction out at every layer and position; it also does not add such a direction to induce refusal.
record.method_sensitivity: The selected head sets depend on the repatching strategy: Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation have low overlap. The paper reports ASR increasing rapidly with a small number of heads and capability degradation beyond approximately 30% of heads. It also notes more gradual ASR growth for Qwen2.5.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation select largely different attention-head sets: overlap is 24.8%, 21.3%, 22.3% and 21.2% (Figure 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention heads whose repatching breaks safety differ depending on the patch value used (mean-harmful vs zero).

fits_no_version.finding: In a Llama3.1-8B case study, zeroing more selected heads moves output from refusal, to mixed refusal with harm, to full compliance, to incoherence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Progressive zeroing of globally selected attention heads shifts a chat model from refusal to compliance, then breaks generation.

fits_no_version.finding: ASR plateaus at about 30% of heads repatched; perplexity rises sharply beyond that point.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Head-repatching jailbreaks saturate at about a third of heads, and larger interventions degrade fluency.

record.problems: The study tests a limited set of open-source models and English-language instructions, as the authors acknowledge. Its interventions target last-token attention-head activations rather than residual-stream directions. The head-overlap evidence is reported as plotted rates without uncertainty estimates, and perplexity is the reported capability-related measure.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. The paper’s attack-comparison tables and its benign/random patching comparison are not extracted because they evaluate the authors’ attack or alternatives rather than directly testing a claim version. Selection heatmaps and optimization losses are omitted because they are used to select heads, not reported behavioral outcomes.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction is computed by the authors. No adding of a direction to induce refusal, and no capability check for direction ablation.
ORTHO capability or coherence is not measured. No released abliterated models are tested. ORTHO settings are unreported (Table 5 lists '-').
No test of whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction. No adversarial training against ablation.
No affine, cone or multi-direction analysis of refusal representations.
Not tested (English only, no base/instruct or cross-variant transfer).

missing.what: ORTHO (refusal-direction weight orthogonalization) ASR per model and benchmark, with vanilla ASR baselines
Benign and random patching comparison: these give only marginal ASR gains over vanilla, while harmful and zero patching exceed 90%

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 link is rejected. The paper's 'distinct pathways' claim concerns which attention heads matter under two patch values, not the geometry of a refusal direction. The V2 evidence is a baseline run with unreported settings and no capability check for ORTHO; weight it lightly.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream direction is found, projected out of every layer and position, or added; no test of refusal on harmless requests or general abilities after that direction intervention.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
The attack repatches selected head activations, not the single refusal direction; no training against ablation is tested.
The study compares attention-head sets and argues for separate pathways, but does not test affine or cone geometry, or a dominant residual-stream direction plus other residual-stream directions.
No separation between harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is measured.
The study tests several model architectures, but does not test transfer of the claimed direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages.
No comparison of refusal-training methods, timing, or stages for whether a removable direction exists.

relation.reason: The ORTHO ASR numbers are the authors' own runs, and they bear on whether orthogonalization removes refusal in released models. This holds only as a comparison baseline, though; the paper does not study the refusal direction itself.

tranche.reason: The paper's only result on a claim version is the ORTHO baseline, which the authors ran (Table 5 lists it among the baselines). It covers four models, three of them not in the original, on AdvBench and StrongREJECT with the HarmBench classifier, so it is a new setting with a result on V2. The reader's T5 is not supported: the paper makes no argument that V2 or any other version is wrong. Its 'separate pathways' finding is about sets of attention heads, not residual-stream directions.

source_check.notes: None of the record's 11 rows covers ORTHO. The 8 ORTHO cells (Table 2) and their vanilla baselines (Table 3) should be added as rows. The text gives no ORTHO details: layer, prompt sets and hyperparameters are all '-', and it is described as activation orthogonalization, so the V2 link rests on the name and the Arditi citation. Separately, the paper is internally inconsistent: the authors' own Llama3.1 StrongREJECT score is 92.01 in Table 2 but 97.44 in Table 3.

statements.correction: arXiv:2601.15801: ORTHO (cited to Arditi et al.; text says it 'orthogonalizes activations' against refusal directions; Table 5 gives no hyperparameters). Judge HarmBench-Llama-2-13b-cls; mean of 3 seeds, no spread reported. AdvBench (520), vanilla (Table 3) -> ORTHO (Table 2): Llama-2-7b-chat 0.38->88.65; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 0.96->94.42; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 1.73->84.81; Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 35.58->82.12. StrongREJECT (313), same order: 0.32->66.77, 1.60->87.22, 7.67->88.50, 29.71->74.44. ORTHO has no capability measure and no control; benign/random patching and perplexity apply only to the authors' attack. Vanilla and ORTHO sit in different tables (3 and 2), with the same benchmarks and judge.
statements.problem: This study's AdvBench numbers are right (Table 2 ORTHO, Table 3 vanilla), but several surrounding claims don't fit it. The text describes ORTHO as orthogonalizing activations, not weights, and gives no harmful/harmless prompt sets. Mistral's untreated baseline (35.58%) isn't low. The conditions list says Qwen2, but this study used Qwen2.5. The judge isn't named. The 'why' credits controls, capability check and uncertainty, but these cover only the authors' head-repatching method, not ORTHO.
